pages.x: At 1:23 in the morning of 26 April 1986, engineers at the Chernobyl power station in Soviet Ukraine were running a safety test on reactor number 4. They had switched off safety systems, and the reactor had a dangerous flaw in its design. Its power suddenly surged. A blast of steam threw off the reactor's huge steel lid, and a second explosion hurled burning fuel into the night.

Firemen from the nearby town of Pripyat climbed onto the roof to fight the flames, with no idea what they faced. Above the reactor the air glowed, and they said it tasted of metal. Within hours they were vomiting, and their skin was burning. Two workers died that night, and 28 more of the first men on the scene died of radiation sickness within weeks.

Pripyat, a new town of about 49,000 people, many of them young families of plant workers, was evacuated the next afternoon. People were told to pack for three days. They never came back. Today trees grow through its flats, and the Ferris wheel of its fairground, due to open that May Day, has never turned for the public.

The Soviet government said nothing. On 28 April alarms went off at the Forsmark nuclear plant in Sweden, more than 1,000 kilometres away, when workers arrived with radioactive dust on their shoes. Swedish scientists traced the wind back to the Soviet Union. That evening Soviet television admitted, in a few seconds on the news, that there had been an accident.

About 600,000 soldiers, miners, firemen and reservists, called liquidators, were sent to clean up. Helicopters dropped thousands of tonnes of sand, lead and boron on the burning reactor. Robots sent onto the roof broke down in the radiation, so soldiers shovelled the debris off by hand, in shifts of a minute or two. By November a concrete shell had been built over the ruin.

Winds carried radiation across Ukraine, Belarus and Russia and over much of Europe. A zone 30 kilometres round the plant was emptied, and thousands of children who drank tainted milk later got thyroid cancer. How many will die of it in the end is still argued over: estimates run from 4,000 to tens of thousands.
pages.of: people moved from their homes for good

pages.x: The disaster, and the first attempts to hide it, shook Mikhail Gorbachev's faith in the Soviet system and pushed him towards glasnost, openness. Twenty years later he wrote that Chernobyl, even more than his own reforms, was perhaps the real cause of the collapse of the Soviet Union.

Chernobyl is the worst nuclear accident in history. It turned many people around the world against nuclear power, and showed that the Soviet system could not be trusted to tell the truth. In 2016 a giant steel arch was slid over the old concrete shell, to keep the ruin safe for a hundred years.
pts: Pripyat has stood empty ever since
